extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing Section 101 patent-eligibility analyses for claims reciting laws of nature, natural phenomena, and nature-based products, including the markedly different characteristics analysis used to identify product-of-nature exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature and Natural Phenomena, Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or that do not have markedly different characteristics compared to what occurs in nature. The courts have often described these exceptions using other terms, including 'physical phenomena,' 'scientific principles', 'natural laws,' and 'products of nature.' The basic tools of scientific and technological work are not patentable because they are part of the storehouse of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Supreme Court and precedent: Funk Bros.; Diamond v. Chakrabarty; Parker v. Flook; O’Reilly v. Morse; Funk. Explains consequence: such subject matter is not patentable under §101 absent further analysis. Use this concept in Step 2A Prong One to identify whether a claim recites one of these judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' Examples of Laws of Nature/Natural Phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have identified specific concepts/products as laws of nature or natural phenomena (non-exhaustive examples provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed by the courts include: (i) isolated DNA (Myriad); (ii) a cloned farm animal (Roslin); (iii) correlation between variations in non-coding regions of DNA and allele presence (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); (iv) metabolism-based correlations (Mayo); (v) correlation between myeloperoxidase in bodily sample and cardiovascular risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health); (vi) electromagnetism to transmit signals (O’Reilly v. Morse); (vii) qualities of bacteria (Funk Bros.); (viii) single-stranded DNA primers (Ambry Genetics); (ix) chemical principle underlying union between fatty elements and water (Tilghman v. Proctor); (x) existence of cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood (Ariosa v. Sequenom); (xi) natural relationship between genotype and drug response (Vanda). Use these as analogies but not as an exhaustive list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Describing Natural Abilities/Responses May Still Be Eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every claim describing a natural ability, quality of a product, or natural process necessarily recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon; claims that are directed to active process steps or applications (rather than mere observation/detection of a natural ability) can be eligible at Prong One.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: process steps for fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes (CellzDirect) found eligible because not focused merely on observing ability to survive freeze-thaw cycles. A method of treating cancer where cancer cells' inability to survive chemotherapy is not considered a law of nature. Method of treating headaches with aspirin — the body's natural response is not a law of nature when claimed as treatment. If such claims recite another exception they require further Prong Two (and Step 2B) analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of Nature Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, courts often refer to the exception as a 'product of nature.' Products of nature include naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A synthetic product that is structurally identical to a natural counterpart is not patent eligible (Ambry Genetics). The key inquiry is whether the claimed product possesses 'markedly different characteristics' from any naturally occurring counterpart. If not, it's a product of nature and requires further Step 2A Prong Two analysis. Examples: Myriad (isolated DNA) and Ambry (primers) described as products of nature; Chakrabarty bacterium not a product of nature because it had markedly different characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics Analysis (Step 2A Prong One)
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to identify product-of-nature exceptions by comparing the claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. It is part of Step 2A Prong One of the Office's eligibility framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as structure, function, and/or other properties and are evaluated case-by-case based on what is recited in the claim. If the claimed nature-based product exhibits markedly different characteristics, it does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B: NO), unless the claim recites another exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Perform the Markedly Different Characteristics Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations in a claim, and avoid over-applying it to claim elements that, when viewed as a whole, are not nature-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, no need to perform the analysis (it is by definition a product-of-nature exception). If the limitation is non-naturally occurring (e.g., due to human intervention), perform the analysis. Consider claim type (product, product-by-process, process) when deciding whether to apply the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to Product Claims and Combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: For product claims, apply the analysis to the entire claimed product. For a nature-based product produced by combining components, analyze the resultant nature-based combination rather than components separately. For claims that combine nature-based products with non-nature elements, apply the analysis only to the nature-based product limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for a claimed 'probiotic composition comprising Lactobacillus and milk' analyze the mixture. For a 'yogurt starter kit comprising Lactobacillus in a container with instructions,' analyze Lactobacillus only; container and instructions are evaluated separately in Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). Funk Bros. shows only the bacterial mixture was analyzed even though other elements were claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-Process Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For product-by-process claims, the analysis focuses on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for more information. The fact that a product is claimed by its process does not avoid the need to compare the product to its natural counterpart for markedly different characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process Claims and When They Are Subject to the Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis because the focus is on active process steps, not products used in those steps. However, if a process claim is drafted so there is no substantive difference from a product claim (i.e., focused on the product itself), then the process claim is subject to the markedly different analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cryopreserving hepatocytes (CellzDirect) was treated as a process claim, not subjected to the product analysis. Conversely, a claim that effectively reads as 'a method of providing an apple' would be treated as focused on the apple (a nature-based product) and subjected to the analysis. Claims to detecting cffDNA were held directed to the cffDNA product (Ariosa/Sequenom context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the Appropriate Naturally Occurring Counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step is selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state to which the claimed nature-based product is compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, that natural thing is the counterpart (e.g., deoxyacid A compared to acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with other naturally co-occurring material (e.g., compare an isolated gene to the gene, not the whole chromosome). If multiple counterparts exist, compare to the closest natural counterpart; examiner should use expertise to select one and, as a best practice, identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if not already clear. For combinations with no natural counterpart, compare to the individual component counterparts (Funk Bros.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Appropriate Characteristics for Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify characteristics to compare that are actually possessed by the claimed product as recited in the claim or encompassed within its broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). Characteristics may be structure, function, and/or other properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product. Examiners determine these from claim language and BRI. Non-limiting types of characteristics include: biological or pharmacological functions/activities (e.g., protein-encoding information, binding ability), chemical and physical properties (e.g., alkalinity, ductility), phenotype (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure/form (physical plasmids, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype). Use case law examples (Myriad, Ambry, Chakrabarty, Parke-Davis, Roslin) to identify relevant characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating Whether Characteristics Are 'Markedly Different'
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'markedly different,' a characteristic must be changed compared to the naturally occurring counterpart and not merely inherent, incidental, or resulting from isolation; the change should generally be caused by applicant's efforts or influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product-of-nature exception. If at least one characteristic changed due to applicant's efforts, it will generally be considered markedly different. Examples: Chakrabarty bacterium (structural—additional plasmids—and functional—degrade multiple hydrocarbons—markedly different → eligible); cDNA (Myriad) structural change (exons only) distinguished from genomic DNA → eligible; isolated genomic BRCA sequences (Myriad): incidental structural changes from isolation were not enough → ineligible. Courts emphasize the difference cannot be merely incidental to isolation or inherent in the natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Markedly Different Characteristics on Eligibility and Further Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics from its natural counterpart, the claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Step 2A (Pathway B: NO), unless the claim recites another judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics, the limitation is a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed) to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or otherwise presents an 'inventive concept.' Examiners should consider recommending claim amendments to narrow the BRI where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner Best Practices Regarding Product-of-Nature Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural and record-keeping practices examiners should follow when performing and documenting markedly different characteristics/product-of-nature analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practices include: identify the selected naturally occurring counterpart in the Office action if not already clear to assist applicant response; point out the broadest reasonable interpretation and recommend possible amendments to narrow claims if a claim is rejected as failing to encompass an inventive concept (Step 2B: NO); consider whether streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP §2106.06) is appropriate for claims that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.
